split_rationale: The source runs about 4,950 words of narration - roughly 38 minutes - across 43 slides, which its two section dividers would make into one 16-minute and one 22-minute package. Three packages instead. Section 1 is the source's own Section I, taken whole: the framework and the blood technique, at about 16 minutes. The source's Section II is split at a genuine seam in the learner's task - collecting each of the remaining specimen types (about 13 minutes), then everything that happens to a specimen once it has been collected (about 9 minutes). That second seam matters because the transport, documentation and waste rules apply to every specimen type equally, and teaching them inside the urine-and-sputum material buries them. Each package carries its own welcome, objectives, summary and results slide as this studio ships.

sme_queries.issue: The yellow and red top vials are both described as biochemistry tubes, with no rule for choosing between them. Slide 13 reads 'YELLOW TOP - Serum separator tube (all biochemistry and microbiology)' and 'RED TOP - No Preservative - Biochemistry test', and the narration says yellow is used for 'most biochemistry tests' while red is 'used for biochemistry and serology tests'. A nurse holding a request for an LFT has two tubes that both claim the test, and the wrong choice is a rejected sample. Please state which tube your laboratory wants for routine biochemistry, and what the other one is reserved for.

Slide 17 contradicts itself on liver function tests. It lists 'LFT: 6 hrs Fasting' and then, two lines later, 'Hematology, Biochemistry, Renal function, Coagulation Profile, Serology: Any time of the day'. An LFT is a biochemistry test, so the slide tells the nurse both to fast the patient for six hours and that no fast is needed. Many laboratories do not require fasting for an LFT at all. Please confirm which applies in your hospital - a nurse following the wrong line will either fast a patient unnecessarily or send a sample that is rejected.

The black top vial for ESR appears in the list of vials on slide 13 but not in the order of draw on slide 11, which runs blood culture, blue, red or yellow, green, purple, grey. A nurse drawing an ESR alongside other tests has no guidance on where it goes in the sequence. Please tell us its position so it can be added to the order-of-draw teaching.

Two different transport windows are given for urine. Slide 23 says to send the specimen 'within 15-20 mins'; the transport table on slide 32 says urine C/S 'within 1 hour'. The storyboard teaches 15 to 20 minutes for a routine specimen and one hour as the outer limit for a culture, which is the reading that makes both true. Please confirm, or give a single figure.

Slide 27 instructs the patient 'not to brush teeth on next day morning' before a sputum collection. Several protocols ask the opposite - brushing without toothpaste, or simply rinsing - to reduce oral flora. The narration hedges with 'according to your protocol', and the storyboard has kept that hedge. Please state your actual instruction so it can be taught plainly.
Slide 29 gives the normal adult CSF volume as 140-170 mL. The figure usually quoted is 125-150 mL. Please confirm the range you want taught.

The speaker notes on slide 18 are truncated - they end mid-sentence at the word 'After'. We have completed the procedure from slide 19's narration, which covers the same steps. Please review the final step of the blood collection slide and confirm nothing was intended beyond documentation and transport.

Slides 18 and 19 both ask the nurse to 'cross check with seniors regarding cost of the blood investigation' and to 'make requisition properly and send for billing'. These are administrative steps specific to your hospital rather than clinical technique. They have been kept, in the preparation step. Please confirm they belong in a clinical module, or tell us to remove them.

Several slides carry text left over from the decks this one was cloned from. 'Indications of Sitz' appears on slide 6; 'myocardial infarction' appears inside the titles of slides 7 to 19; 'ture of Water' appears in slide 22's title; 'Role of Nurse in radiology department' appears on slide 31; and a text box reading 'Abnormal muscle function' appears on slides 22 to 31. All of it has been excluded. Please confirm none of it was intended content.

Slide 31 carries only two headings on screen - 'NASOPHARYNGEAL SWAB' and 'OROPHARYNGEAL SWAB' - with the entire technique for both in the speaker notes. We have built the on-screen content from that narration. Please review the resulting slide and confirm the technique as written, particularly the insertion direction for the nasopharyngeal swab.

modules.title: Section 1: Understanding Pathology and Blood Collection

objectives.text: Define pathology and explain why specimen collection decides the result
Describe the three phases of laboratory testing and name the one where most errors occur

slides.heading: Patient Preparation and Specimen Collection
slides.design_rationale: Cover. A nurse at the bedside with a collection tray, because the module's whole argument is that the result is decided at the bedside rather than in the laboratory.

images.purpose: Nurse at a patient's bedside with a phlebotomy tray and labelled tubes

candidates.shows: Phlebotomy photos - prefer one showing labelled tubes and a tray

vo: Welcome to the module on Patient Preparation and Specimen Collection for Nurses, prepared by Bodhi Learning Labs.
Accurate diagnosis begins long before the laboratory report is generated. It starts at the bedside, with proper patient preparation and correct specimen collection.
A simple mistake - the wrong label, improper fasting, a delayed transport - leads to an inaccurate result and inappropriate treatment.
In this first section you will learn what pathology testing is, where errors actually occur, and how to take a blood sample that the laboratory can use.

slides.heading: Learning objectives
slides.design_rationale: Objectives revealed one per narration line, scoped to this section. The other specimen types and the post-collection handling are taught in Sections 2 and 3.

images.purpose: Simple line-art target or goal icon, single colour

candidates.shows: Icon library - pick a single-colour outline target

vo: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
Define pathology and explain why specimen collection decides the result.
Describe the three phases of laboratory testing and name the one where most errors occur.
Identify a patient correctly before collecting any specimen.
Apply the order of draw and select the correct vial for a given test.
State the fasting and timing requirements for the common blood tests.
And collect a blood sample by the correct technique.
slides.dev_notes: Objectives in later sections: urine, sputum, stool, CSF and swab collection (Section 2); transport, documentation, complications, education and waste (Section 3).

slides.heading: What this course covers
slides.design_rationale: The source menu lists twenty-four sub-topics on one screen, which is an index rather than a choice. Collapsed to three sections, each chip naming what sits behind it, so the learner sees three doors rather than twenty-four.

chunks.label: Understanding pathology and blood collection
chunks.body: Definition and importance · the three laboratory phases · patient identification · order of draw · vials · fasting and timing · taking the sample

chunks.label: Collecting urine, sputum, stool, CSF and swabs
chunks.body: Routine and culture urine · 24-hour collection · sputum · stool · lumbar puncture · nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swabs

slides.dev_notes: Menu - each chip jumps to that section's package.
vo: The course menu is displayed.

This course runs in three sections: understanding pathology and blood collection; collecting urine, sputum, stool, cerebrospinal fluid and swabs; and what happens to a specimen after you have taken it.
Click on a section to proceed.

slides.heading: What is pathology?
slides.design_rationale: One idea stated precisely. The source's definition runs together the academic discipline and the laboratory work a nurse actually meets, and separating them is what makes the rest of the module make sense.

chunks.label: Pathology
chunks.body: The branch of medical science that studies the causes and effects of disease and injury

chunks.label: In practice
chunks.body: The laboratory testing of blood, urine, stool, body fluids and tissue used for diagnosis and treatment

chunks.label: Pathologist
chunks.body: The physician who specialises in this field

images.purpose: Laboratory scientist examining a specimen under a microscope

candidates.shows: Laboratory photos - prefer a clinical rather than research setting

vo: Pathology is the branch of medical science that studies the causes and effects of diseases and injuries. It explains how disease develops and how it affects tissues and organs.
In day-to-day practice, the word also means the laboratory testing of blood, urine, stool, body fluids and tissue samples, used for diagnosis and treatment.
A doctor who specialises in this field is called a pathologist.

slides.heading: What gets tested
slides.design_rationale: Seven specimen types, each with its own collection technique later in the course. Icons so they read as a set the learner will meet one by one, with blood marked as the one they will take most often.

chunks.label: Blood
chunks.body: The commonest specimen

callouts.text: Pathology tests help prevent, diagnose, manage and monitor allergies, infections, chronic disease and cancer. The sample you take is the first step in all of that.

vo: A pathology test examines a sample taken from the body.
Blood is the commonest specimen, and the one you will collect most often.
Urine, stool, body fluids, sputum, swabs and tissue biopsies are all also sent for testing.
These tests give the information that lets doctors diagnose disease, plan treatment and monitor progress - detecting infection, allergy, chronic disease and cancer.

slides.heading: The three phases of laboratory testing
slides.design_rationale: Three phases in sequence, and the whole point of the slide is which one belongs to the nurse. A numbered track with the pre-analytical phase expanded, because every task in that phase is a task the source lists elsewhere as a nursing responsibility.

chunks.label: Pre-analytical
chunks.body: Patient preparation · correct collection · proper labelling · timely transport

chunks.label: Analytical
chunks.body: Processing and testing in the laboratory

chunks.label: Post-analytical
chunks.body: Reporting and interpretation of results

callouts.text: Errors can occur in any phase, but most occur in the pre-analytical one - which is the phase you own. Wrong timing or wrong technique produces a wrong result, a repeat test, and a delayed treatment.

vo: Laboratory testing is divided into three phases.
The pre-analytical phase includes patient preparation, correct specimen collection, proper labelling and timely transport to the laboratory.
The analytical phase is the processing and testing of the specimen in the laboratory.
The post-analytical phase is the reporting and interpretation of the results.

Errors can occur in any phase, but most occur during the pre-analytical phase - which makes the nurse's role the decisive one. A sample collected at the wrong time or by the wrong technique gives a misleading result, forces a repeat test, adds to the patient's discomfort, and delays the start of treatment.

slides.heading: Patient identification
slides.design_rationale: The single most consequential check in the whole module, and the one the source itself marks 'very important'. A definition slide rather than a bullet in a list, so the rule and the prohibition sit together and neither can be skimmed.

chunks.label: Use at least two identifiers
chunks.body: Patient name · UHID or MRN number · date of birth

chunks.label: Match them against
chunks.body: The laboratory request form and the patient's identification band

callouts.text: Never collect a specimen without confirming identity. A misidentified sample produces a correct result attached to the wrong patient, which is more dangerous than no result at all.

images.purpose: Nurse checking a patient's identification wristband

vo: Correct patient identification is the most important step before collecting any specimen.
Always use at least two identifiers - the patient's full name, the UHID or medical record number, and the date of birth.
Match these details against the laboratory request form and the patient's identification band.
And never collect a specimen without confirming identity, because misidentification leads directly to diagnostic and treatment errors.

slides.heading: Standard precautions
slides.design_rationale: Five precautions that apply to every collection in the course, placed before any technique is taught so they are the frame rather than an afterthought.

chunks.label: Wear gloves and PPE as needed

vo: Standard precautions apply to every specimen collection procedure.
Perform hand hygiene before and after the procedure.
Wear gloves and other personal protective equipment as needed.
Use sterile equipment wherever it is required.
Dispose of needles and other sharps safely, in puncture-proof containers.
And clean any spill immediately with an appropriate disinfectant.

slides.heading: The order of draw
slides.design_rationale: Six tubes in a fixed sequence, and the sequence is the entire content - fill them in the wrong order and additive carries from one tube into the next. A numbered track makes the order unmissable, with each tube's purpose expanded behind it.

callouts.text: The order exists to stop additive from one tube carrying into the next. Drawing out of sequence changes the result without changing anything you can see.

vo: The order of draw is the sequence in which blood collection tubes are filled during a venipuncture, and following it matters because it prevents additive carrying over from one tube to the next and altering the result.

slides.heading: What each tube is for
slides.design_rationale: The expanded state of the order-of-draw track. Each panel carries the additive and the test, which is the pairing a nurse needs at the trolley, with the reasoning in the narration so no panel becomes a paragraph.

chunks.label: 1 - Blood culture
chunks.body: First, to maintain sterility and avoid contamination.

chunks.label: 2 - Citrate, blue
chunks.body: Sodium citrate. Coagulation - PT, INR, APTT. Fill to the exact marked level.

chunks.label: 3 - Serum, red or yellow
chunks.body: Plain, or clot activator and gel. Biochemistry, LFT, KFT, serology.

chunks.label: 4 - Heparin, green
chunks.body: Heparin. Electrolytes and special chemistry.

chunks.label: 5 - EDTA, purple
chunks.body: EDTA binds calcium to prevent clotting. CBC, haemoglobin, blood grouping.

chunks.label: 6 - Fluoride, grey
chunks.body: Sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate. Glucose - it prevents glycolysis.

vo: The first tube is the blood culture bottle. It is collected first to maintain sterility and avoid contamination, which matters most when infection is suspected.

Second is the citrate tube, with a blue cap. It contains sodium citrate and is used for coagulation tests such as PT, INR and APTT. This tube must be filled to the exact marked level or the result will be wrong.

Third is the serum tube, with a red or yellow cap. It may be plain or contain a clot activator and gel separator, and it is used for biochemistry, liver function tests, kidney function tests and serology.
Fourth is the heparin tube, with a green cap. It is used for electrolyte testing and some special chemistry tests.
Fifth is the EDTA tube, with a purple or lavender cap, used for haematology tests such as complete blood count, haemoglobin and blood grouping. EDTA prevents clotting by binding calcium.
And last is the fluoride tube, with a grey cap. It contains sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate, and is used mainly for blood glucose, because it prevents glycolysis.

slides.heading: Check your understanding!
slides.instruction: Select the correct answer and click Submit.
slides.design_rationale: The source's own scenario, placed immediately after the track. It gives a realistic set of requests rather than asking for the sequence in the abstract, which is how the order is actually used.
slides.question: A nurse is collecting blood samples for a patient requiring the following investigations: Blood culture, PT/INR, Liver Function Test (LFT), Complete Blood Count (CBC), and Blood Glucose. To prevent contamination of additives, which sequence should the nurse follow?

options.text: Blood Culture → Blue → Red/Yellow → Purple → Gray
Red → Blue → Purple → Gray → Blood Culture
Purple → Red → Blue → Gray → Blood Culture
Gray → Purple → Green → Red → Blue

slides.rationale: The recommended order of draw prevents additive carryover between tubes. Blood cultures are collected first, followed by citrate (blue), serum (red/yellow), EDTA (purple) and fluoride (gray). No heparin test is requested here, so the green tube does not appear.
vo: Now, let us answer a question to check our understanding.

A nurse is collecting blood samples for a patient requiring a blood culture, PT and INR, a liver function test, a complete blood count, and blood glucose. To prevent contamination of additives, which sequence should the nurse follow?
Select the correct answer and click Submit.

slides.heading: The vials and what they are for
slides.design_rationale: Colour against additive against test against whether to mix - four variables a nurse holds at the trolley, and the source wrote them as seven run-on lines. The mixing column matters because shaking the wrong tube haemolyses the sample.

rows: Clot activator and gel - serum separator
Do not shake - allow to clot
Fill to the mark, then invert gently

images.purpose: Rack of blood collection tubes showing the different coloured caps
images.search_terms: blood collection tubes coloured caps rack vacutainer

candidates.shows: Tube-rack photos - prefer one where every cap colour is distinguishable

callouts.text: Invert, never shake. Vigorous shaking haemolyses the sample and the laboratory will reject it.

vo: Each vial contains a specific additive that preserves the sample for a particular kind of test.
The yellow top is a serum separator tube containing clot activator and gel, used for most biochemistry tests and for some microbiology and serology.
The red top is a plain tube with no preservative, used for biochemistry and serology. It should not be shaken - the blood is allowed to clot naturally.

The purple or lavender top contains EDTA, an anticoagulant, and is used for haematology tests such as complete blood count, haemoglobin and peripheral smear. Invert it gently several times after collection.
The grey top contains sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate and is used mainly for glucose, because the fluoride prevents blood cells breaking the glucose down. Mix it gently.
The blue top contains sodium citrate and is used for coagulation studies such as PT, INR and APTT. It must be filled to the correct level and inverted gently.
The green top contains heparin and is used for ammonia and certain special chemistry tests.
And the black top contains sodium citrate and is used specifically for erythrocyte sedimentation rate, by the Westergren method.

slides.heading: Why a specimen gets rejected
slides.design_rationale: Seven reasons, every one of them preventable at the bedside. Icons so they read as a pre-send checklist rather than as a list of laboratory rules.

callouts.text: Every rejection means a second needle for the patient. Checking the label, the fill level and the container before you send costs seconds.

vo: Laboratories reject specimens that do not meet quality requirements, and every rejection means the patient is stuck again.
Specimens are rejected for incorrect or missing labels.
For haemolysis.
For insufficient quantity.
For use of the wrong container.
For contamination.
For delayed transport.
And for clotting in a sample that should have been anticoagulated, such as a CBC specimen.

slides.heading: What changes a result
slides.design_rationale: Eight patient factors that alter a result without altering the technique. Given their own slide because the nurse's job here is to ask and to document rather than to do anything differently.

callouts.text: You cannot change most of these. You can ask about them and record them, which is what lets the result be interpreted correctly.

vo: Many factors influence laboratory results without anything being wrong with the technique.
The patient's fasting status, their current medications, their body posture, recent exercise, emotional stress, smoking, alcohol intake, and the menstrual cycle all affect particular tests.

If these are not taken into account, the result may be altered and misinterpreted. So give the patient proper instructions beforehand, and document any relevant factor before the specimen is collected.

slides.heading: Tests that need something extra
slides.design_rationale: Five tests, each with a handling rule that nothing else in the course requires. A table pairs the test with the rule, where the source's indented list left the learner to work out which rule belonged to which test.

rows: Collect before antibiotics. Strict aseptic technique. Two separate sites.
Antibiotics suppress growth; two sites improve detection
Cooling slows cell metabolism and preserves the values
The level rises quickly if the sample is not handled properly
A prolonged tourniquet falsely raises the lactate
A single value cannot show the rise and fall of cardiac injury

callouts.text: Blood cultures before antibiotics, every time. Once the first dose is in, the chance of growing the organism falls sharply and the patient may be treated blind.

vo: Some tests need handling that nothing else does.
Blood cultures should always be collected before antibiotics are started, using strict aseptic technique and preferably from two separate sites, which improves the detection of infection.
Arterial blood gas samples should be transported on ice if there is any delay in processing.
Ammonia samples must go to the laboratory immediately, on ice, because the level rises quickly if the sample is mishandled.
Lactate samples should be collected without prolonged tourniquet application, which falsely raises the lactate.
And troponin is usually performed as a series at specific intervals, because the pattern over time is what identifies heart muscle injury.

slides.heading: Fasting and timing
slides.design_rationale: Test against requirement - the question a nurse is asked by a patient the night before, and the one that most often produces a wasted sample. A table is the only shape that answers it at a glance.

rows: Haematology, biochemistry, renal function, coagulation, serology
Any time of day, unless the physician specifies otherwise

callouts.text: A postprandial sugar taken at 90 minutes or 3 hours is not a PPBS. The timing is the test.

vo: Different blood tests need different timing and fasting.
For a fasting blood sugar, the patient fasts for at least six hours.
A random blood sugar can be collected at any time of day.
A postprandial blood sugar is collected exactly two hours after a meal - the timing is what makes it that test.
A liver function test is usually done after six hours of fasting.
A lipid profile requires twelve hours of fasting for an accurate cholesterol and triglyceride measurement.
And haematology, routine biochemistry, renal function tests, coagulation profile and serology can generally be collected at any time of day, unless the physician specifies otherwise.

slides.heading: Collecting a blood sample
slides.design_rationale: The core procedure, as a numbered track. The order carries real safety - identification before articles, labelling and explanation before the needle - so the sequence stays visible while the detail is explored.

chunks.label: Fill the vial and mix if required

vo: Blood sample collection follows a set sequence, and each step protects either the patient or the sample. Nine steps, in this order.

slides.heading: What each step requires
slides.design_rationale: The expanded state of the collection track. The technique details that decide whether the laboratory can use the sample - tourniquet position, not opening the vacuum cap, the fill mark - live here rather than on the track itself.

chunks.label: Check the order
chunks.body: Verify the physician's advice and the investigations required. Complete the requisition and send for billing. Obtain consent or clearance where needed.

chunks.label: Identify the patient
chunks.body: At least two identifiers, matched to the request form and the wristband.

chunks.label: Prepare articles
chunks.body: Syringes or vacutainers, tourniquet, alcohol swabs, gloves, labels and the correct tubes. Check the vial with a senior if unsure.

chunks.label: Label the sample
chunks.body: Barcode or patient details, per hospital policy.

chunks.label: Prepare the patient
chunks.body: Explain the procedure to reduce anxiety and gain cooperation.

chunks.label: Hand hygiene and gloves
chunks.body: Then apply the tourniquet about two inches above the chosen vein.

chunks.label: Clean and collect
chunks.body: Clean with an alcohol swab and let it dry. Insert the needle and draw in the correct order.

chunks.label: Fill and mix
chunks.body: Do not open the vial cap - puncture it and let the vacuum draw. Check the blood reaches the mark. Invert gently; do not shake.

chunks.label: Document and transport
chunks.body: Lab register, billing card, nursing notes and patient file. Send with the requisition.

callouts.text: A vacuum tube fills itself. Forcing blood in, or pushing hard on the plunger, haemolyses the sample and wastes the draw.

vo: First, review the physician's order and confirm the investigations required. Verify the cost where your unit requires it, complete the requisition, and obtain any consent or administrative clearance before the sample is sent.
Identify the patient using at least two identifiers, matched against the request form and the identification band.

Gather all the articles you need and take them to the bedside - syringes or vacutainers, tourniquet, alcohol swabs, gloves, labels and the correct collection tubes. If you are unsure which vial a test needs, check with a senior nurse or the laboratory rather than guessing.
Label the tubes with the barcode or the patient's details, according to hospital policy.
Explain the procedure to the patient to reduce anxiety and gain cooperation, and obtain verbal or written consent where it is required.
Perform hand hygiene and put on disposable gloves, then apply the tourniquet about two inches above the vein you have chosen.
Clean the site with an alcohol swab and allow it to dry. Insert the needle and collect the sample in the correct order of draw.

Transfer the blood into the appropriate vial. With a vacuum tube, do not remove the cap - puncture the rubber stopper and let the vacuum draw the blood in. Check that the blood has reached the fill mark, which matters most for coagulation tubes, and invert gently if mixing is required.
Finally, document in the laboratory register, the billing card, the nursing notes and the patient file, and send the sample to the laboratory with the completed requisition form.

slides.design_rationale: The source's own scenario, closing the section. Every distractor is a shortcut a busy nurse might take, which is what makes it worth asking.
slides.question: A nurse is preparing to collect a blood sample for a patient's coagulation profile (PT/INR). While checking the patient's identity, she notices that the UHID on the laboratory request form does not match the patient's wristband. What should the nurse do first?

Ask the patient's relative to confirm the patient's identity.
Stop the procedure, verify the patient's identity using two identifiers, and resolve the discrepancy before collecting the specimen.
Collect the sample and relabel it after confirmation.

slides.rationale: Correct patient identification is the first and most critical step in specimen collection. Collection must not proceed until the discrepancy has been resolved, because a sample attached to the wrong patient causes diagnostic and treatment errors.

slides.design_rationale: Added. Fasting is what the patient asks about the night before, and the error is specific - applying one test's rule to another. A match tests exactly that pairing.

chunks.label: Fasting blood sugar
chunks.body: 6 hours fasting

chunks.label: Lipid profile
chunks.body: 12 hours fasting

chunks.label: Postprandial blood sugar
chunks.body: Exactly 2 hours after a meal

chunks.label: Random blood sugar
chunks.body: Any time of day

slides.rationale: Six hours for a fasting sugar, twelve for a lipid profile because triglycerides take longer to clear, exactly two hours after a meal for a postprandial sugar - the timing is the test - and any time for a random sugar.
vo: Now, let us answer a question to check our understanding.

slides.heading: Check your understanding!
slides.instruction: Select all that apply and click Submit.
slides.design_rationale: Added. Technique errors travel in groups rather than singly, so a multi-select asks the learner to recognise several at once - which is how they appear when a sample comes back rejected.
slides.question: A coagulation sample is returned by the laboratory as unusable. Which of these could have caused it? Select all that apply.

options.text: The citrate tube was filled only halfway
The tube was shaken vigorously to mix it
The sample was drawn from a vein above a running IV infusion
The tube was inverted gently four times after filling

slides.rationale: A, B and C. An underfilled citrate tube has the wrong blood-to-additive ratio, vigorous shaking haemolyses the sample, and IV fluid dilutes it. Gentle inversion is the correct way to mix the tube.

slides.heading: Section 1 in brief
slides.design_rationale: A recap in the order taught, consolidating the framework and the blood technique before the other specimen types begin.

chunks.label: Pathology testing of blood, urine, stool, fluids and tissue is what diagnosis rests on.
Three phases - and most errors happen in the pre-analytical one, which is yours.
Two identifiers, matched to the form and the band, before any specimen.
Order of draw: culture, blue, red or yellow, green, purple, grey.
The cap colour names the additive, and the additive names the test.
FBS and LFT 6 hours, lipid profile 12 hours, PPBS exactly 2 hours after a meal.
Do not open a vacuum cap, fill to the mark, invert - never shake.

vo: Let us consolidate this section before moving on.
Pathology testing of blood, urine, stool, body fluids and tissue is what diagnosis, treatment and monitoring rest on.
Laboratory testing has three phases, and most errors occur in the pre-analytical phase - the one the nurse owns.
Use at least two identifiers, matched against the request form and the identification band, before collecting any specimen.
The order of draw is blood culture, blue citrate, red or yellow serum, green heparin, purple EDTA, grey fluoride.
The cap colour tells you the additive, and the additive tells you which test the tube is for.
Fasting blood sugar and liver function tests need six hours, a lipid profile needs twelve, and a postprandial sugar is taken exactly two hours after a meal.
And at the bedside: never open a vacuum cap, always fill to the mark, and invert gently rather than shaking.
In Section 2 you will learn to collect urine, sputum, stool, cerebrospinal fluid and swabs.

vo: Welcome to Section 2 of the module on Patient Preparation and Specimen Collection.
Each specimen type has its own container, its own timing and its own technique - and most of the errors that reach the laboratory come from mixing them up.
In this section you will learn to collect urine for routine examination and for culture, a twenty-four-hour collection, sputum, stool, cerebrospinal fluid, and nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swabs.

slides.heading: Learning objectives
slides.design_rationale: Objectives for the collection section, each naming a procedure the learner will be observed performing.

images.purpose: Simple line-art target or goal icon, single colour

candidates.shows: Icon library - pick a single-colour outline target

vo: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
Collect a midstream urine specimen for routine examination.
Collect urine for culture and sensitivity, including from a Foley catheter.
Carry out a 24-hour urine collection correctly.
Collect sputum and stool specimens by the correct technique.
Assist with a lumbar puncture and care for the patient afterwards.
And collect nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swabs.

slides.heading: The urine tests
slides.design_rationale: Five urine tests that look alike on a request form and are collected completely differently. Named as a set first, so the learner knows which procedure they are about to need.

chunks.label: Urine R/E and M/E
chunks.body: Colour, specific gravity, protein, sugar, cells and crystals

chunks.label: Urine C/S
chunks.body: Identifies the organism and the effective antibiotic

chunks.label: 24-hour urine for protein
chunks.body: Total protein or creatinine over a full day

chunks.label: Spot sodium
chunks.body: Sodium excretion, collected stat

chunks.label: Microalbumin
chunks.body: Early kidney damage in diabetes and hypertension

vo: Urine tests assess kidney function, detect infection and identify metabolic disorders.
Urine for routine and microscopic examination evaluates colour, specific gravity, protein, sugar, and microscopic elements such as cells and crystals.
Urine for culture and sensitivity identifies the organism causing an infection and determines which antibiotic will work.
A twenty-four-hour collection measures substances such as protein and creatinine across a full day.
Spot sodium assesses sodium excretion and is collected at any time.
And microalbumin is a sensitive test for early kidney damage, particularly in patients with diabetes and hypertension.

slides.heading: Collecting a routine urine specimen
slides.design_rationale: Seven steps, several of which happen the night before. A numbered track so the preparation that has to precede the collection is visible as part of the procedure rather than as advice.

chunks.label: Inform the patient the previous night
Leave the container at the bedside
Explain perineal cleaning with soap and water

callouts.text: Midstream means the patient starts to void, discards the first portion, then collects. The first portion carries the contaminants the test is trying to avoid.

images.purpose: Sterile screw-capped urine specimen container with a label
images.search_terms: urine specimen container screw cap sterile

vo: Inform the patient the previous night, especially when an early morning specimen is needed, and leave a clean, labelled container at the bedside.
Explain that they should wash the perineal area with soap and water to reduce contamination.
Early morning urine is preferred because it is more concentrated and gives more reliable results.
After cleaning, the patient begins to void, discards the first portion, then collects the midstream urine in a clean, screw-capped container. This is the midstream clean-catch technique.
Perform hand hygiene before and after handling the specimen.
Label the container immediately with the patient's details and the date and time of collection.
Then document in the pathology register and send the specimen with the requisition form within fifteen to twenty minutes, before the urine composition changes and bacteria multiply.

slides.heading: Urine for culture and sensitivity
slides.design_rationale: Two completely different techniques depending on whether the patient has a catheter, set side by side because choosing the wrong one produces a contaminated sample and an antibiotic the patient did not need.

chunks.label: Patient can void
chunks.body:
Sterile screw-capped container.
Same midstream clean-catch method as for a routine specimen.

chunks.label: Patient has a Foley catheter
chunks.body:
Clamp the tubing below the port for 20–30 minutes.
Clean the port with an alcohol swab.
Aspirate with a sterile syringe through the sampling port.

callouts.text: Never collect urine for culture from the drainage bag. Bag urine is colonised and will grow organisms that are not infecting the patient.

vo: Urine for culture and sensitivity identifies the organism causing a urinary tract infection and determines the most effective antibiotic. It must always be collected in a sterile, screw-capped container.
For a patient who can void normally, the method is the same midstream clean-catch technique - clean the perineal area, discard the first part of the urine, and collect the midstream portion.

If the patient has a Foley catheter, never collect from the drainage bag, because it is contaminated. Clamp the catheter tubing below the sampling port for twenty to thirty minutes so fresh urine collects. Clean the sampling port with an alcohol swab and let it dry. Then aspirate urine from the port with a sterile syringe and transfer it to the sterile container.

Wherever possible, collect the sample before antibiotics are started, which improves the chance of identifying the organism. Label it and send it to the laboratory immediately with the requisition form.

slides.heading: Check your understanding!
slides.instruction: Select the correct answer and click Submit.
slides.design_rationale: The source's own question, placed straight after the comparison. Option A is the shortcut that is actually taken on busy wards, which is precisely why it is worth testing.
slides.question: A patient with an indwelling Foley catheter requires a urine sample for culture and sensitivity (C/S). What is the correct method of specimen collection?

options.text: Collect urine from the drainage bag.
Remove the catheter and collect the first urine.
Clamp the catheter, disinfect the sampling port, and collect urine using a sterile syringe.
Ask the patient to void around the catheter.

slides.rationale: Urine for culture should never be collected from the drainage bag, because it is contaminated. Fresh urine is obtained aseptically from the sampling port after clamping the catheter.
vo: Now, let us answer a question to check our understanding.
A patient with an indwelling Foley catheter requires a urine sample for culture and sensitivity. What is the correct method of specimen collection?
Select the correct answer and click Submit.

slides.heading: The 24-hour urine collection
slides.design_rationale: A collection that runs for a day across several shifts, where one missed void invalidates the whole thing. A numbered track, because the discard-and-start-the-clock step is the one everybody gets wrong.

chunks.label: Obtain the jar from the laboratory and label it
Ask the patient to void - discard this urine
Record that time: the 24 hours start here
Collect every void into the jar for 24 hours
At the same time next day, collect the final specimen
Close the jar and send it with the requisition

callouts.text: The first urine is discarded and the clock starts then. Including it - or missing a single void during the day - makes the whole 24-hour result wrong.

slides.dev_notes: Spot sodium and microalbumin are stat collections - any time, clean labelled container, sent promptly. Carried in the narration of this slide.
vo: Spot sodium and microalbumin are stat samples - collected at any time of day as ordered, in a clean labelled container, and sent promptly.
A twenty-four-hour urine for protein is different, and it is the one most often spoiled.
Follow the physician's order, and obtain the special collection jar from the laboratory. Label it with the patient's details and the start time.
At the beginning of the test, ask the patient to empty the bladder completely - and discard that urine.
Record the exact time, because that is when the twenty-four hours begin.
After that, collect every urine the patient passes for the next twenty-four hours in the laboratory jar. Instruct the patient or caregiver to tell you each time they void, so none is missed.
At the same time on the following day, collect the final specimen and add it to the container.
Close the lid securely and send the whole specimen to the laboratory with the requisition form. Accurate timing and complete collection are what make the result meaningful.

slides.heading: Collecting sputum
slides.design_rationale: Seven steps, and the whole procedure turns on one distinction the patient has to be taught - sputum from the chest, not saliva from the mouth. A numbered track with that distinction lifted into a warning.

chunks.label: Inform the patient the previous night
Leave a sterile container at the bedside
Next morning, rinse the mouth with plain water

callouts.text: Saliva is not sputum. The sample should be thick and mucoid - watery saliva will be rejected or will grow mouth flora instead of the pathogen.

vo: Sputum for Gram stain and culture identifies the organism causing a respiratory infection.
Inform the patient the previous night and, according to your protocol, advise them not to brush their teeth on the morning of collection. Leave a sterile, screw-capped container at the bedside.
Early morning sputum is preferred, because secretions accumulate overnight and give a better sample.
Ask the patient to rinse the mouth thoroughly with plain water, to remove food particles and reduce contamination.
Instruct them to take two or three deep breaths, then cough deeply from the chest to bring up sputum from the lungs - not saliva from the mouth or throat.
The sputum should be expectorated directly into the sterile container, and it should be thick and mucoid rather than watery.
Close the container securely, label it with the patient's details and the date and time, and send it to the laboratory promptly with the requisition form.

slides.heading: Stool specimens
slides.design_rationale: Three tests with three completely different rules, including drug holds that start a week before. A table pairs each test with its own instruction, where the source's single list made them look interchangeable.

rows: Stool for OPC - ova, parasite, cyst
Three samples on three different days
1–3 days between samples. To the laboratory within 2 hours
Stool for OBT - occult blood test
Stop NSAIDs - aspirin, ibuprofen, indomethacin - for 7 days. Stop iron for 3 days. Collect 3 days before or after menstruation

callouts.text: The occult blood drug holds are stopped only on medical advice. Seven days without aspirin is a clinical decision, not a laboratory one.

vo: Stool specimens are collected for different purposes, and each test has its own instructions.
For stool for ova, parasite and cyst, collect three samples on three different days, with one to three days between collections, and send each sample to the laboratory within two hours.
For stool routine examination, collect a small, fresh sample, and avoid sending the specimen at night so it can be processed in time.

For the occult blood test, NSAIDs such as aspirin, ibuprofen and indomethacin are stopped for seven days and iron supplements for three days, where that is medically advised. In women, the sample is not collected during menstruation - take it three days before or after the period.
Always collect stool in a clean, dry, labelled container and send it promptly.

slides.heading: Cerebrospinal fluid
slides.design_rationale: The one specimen in the course the nurse does not collect. Defined on its own slide so the division of responsibility - clinician collects, nurse prepares and monitors - is explicit before the articles and the aftercare are taught.

chunks.label: What it is
chunks.body: Clear fluid in the subarachnoid space, surrounding the brain in the skull and the spinal cord in the spinal column

chunks.label: Normal volume
chunks.body: Adult 140–170 mL · child 10–60 mL

chunks.label: Who collects it
chunks.body: A trained clinician only, by lumbar puncture, under strict aseptic precautions

callouts.text: Your part is preparation, positioning, asepsis, monitoring and immediate transport. The needle is not yours, but everything around it is.

images.purpose: Lumbar puncture tray set out with needles, syringes and specimen bottles
images.search_terms: lumbar puncture tray sterile needles bottles

candidates.shows: LP tray photos - prefer a laid-out sterile tray

vo: Cerebrospinal fluid is a clear fluid in the subarachnoid space, surrounding the brain and spinal cord. It cushions and protects the central nervous system and helps transport nutrients and waste.
The normal volume in an adult is approximately one hundred and forty to one hundred and seventy millilitres, and in a child ten to sixty millilitres.
CSF is collected only by a trained clinician, by lumbar puncture, under strict aseptic precautions.

slides.heading: Articles to have ready
slides.design_rationale: Five items the nurse assembles before the clinician arrives. Icons so the tray can be checked at a glance, which is how it is actually done.

chunks.label: Labelled sterile containers for the fluid

callouts.text: Label the containers before the procedure starts. CSF is numbered in the order the bottles are filled, and that order is part of the result.

vo: Prepare all the necessary articles before the procedure begins.
Lumbar puncture needles of appropriate sizes, and sterile syringes.
Local anaesthetic, such as Lidocaine or Xylocaine.
A sterile cut sheet, a dressing trolley, antiseptic solution and sterile gloves.
And properly labelled sterile containers for the CSF.
During the procedure, the nurse assists with positioning the patient, monitors vital signs, maintains asepsis, and makes sure the specimen goes to the laboratory immediately.

slides.heading: After the lumbar puncture
slides.design_rationale: Four actions in the recovery period, where the complication the patient will remember - the headache - is the one preventable by positioning. A numbered track with that lifted into a warning.

chunks.label: Lie flat for at least 30 minutes
Check vital signs and neurological status
Elevate the foot end of the bed if ordered
Blood sugar after LP if ordered

callouts.text: Watch the puncture site for CSF leak or bleeding, and ask the patient to report headache, nausea, dizziness or back pain.

vo: After the lumbar puncture, help the patient lie flat for at least thirty minutes, or as your protocol specifies, to reduce the risk of a post-lumbar-puncture headache. Encourage them to report any headache, nausea, dizziness or back pain.
Monitor vital signs regularly, observe the puncture site for leakage of cerebrospinal fluid or bleeding, and check the neurological status and level of consciousness.
In some settings the foot end of the bed is elevated, according to physician preference or institutional policy.
A blood glucose sample may be collected after the procedure if ordered, because it is compared with the CSF glucose level.
Keep the patient comfortable, encourage oral fluids if not contraindicated, document the procedure and the observations, and report any abnormal finding immediately.

slides.heading: Check your understanding!
slides.instruction: Select the correct answer and click Submit.
slides.design_rationale: The source's own question, placed right after the aftercare track so the positioning rule is tested while it is still in front of the learner.
slides.question: Following a lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, which nursing intervention is most appropriate to reduce the risk of post-lumbar puncture headache?

options.text: Encourage the patient to walk immediately after the procedure.
Position the patient flat in bed as per institutional protocol and monitor vital signs.
Place the patient in a high Fowler's position.
Restrict all oral fluids for the next six hours.

slides.rationale: After CSF collection the patient remains flat for the recommended period, while the nurse monitors vital signs and neurological status - which reduces the risk of headache and detects complications early.
vo: Now, let us answer a question to check our understanding.

slides.heading: Nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swabs
slides.design_rationale: Two techniques that sound similar and go to completely different places. The source slide carried only the two headings with the whole technique in narration, so the content is built here from the narration and set side by side - the direction of insertion is the part that is got wrong.

chunks.label: Nasopharyngeal
chunks.body:
Blow the nose; head tilted slightly back.
Insert the flexible swab parallel to the palate.
Straight back towards the ear, not upward.
Advance until resistance; rotate gently.
Leave a few seconds, then withdraw slowly.

chunks.label: Oropharyngeal
chunks.body:
Open wide and say 'Ahh'.
Tongue depressor if needed.
Rub both tonsillar pillars and the posterior pharynx.
Avoid the tongue, teeth and gums.

callouts.text: Directed upward instead of straight back, a nasopharyngeal swab is painful and samples the wrong place. Parallel to the palate, towards the ear.

vo: Nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swabs diagnose respiratory infections such as influenza, COVID-19 and bacterial throat infections.

For a nasopharyngeal swab, the direction of insertion is what matters. Parallel to the palate and straight back towards the ear - angled upward, the swab is painful and samples the wrong place. Advance until you feel resistance at the nasopharynx, rotate gently to absorb secretions, then withdraw slowly.
For an oropharyngeal swab, the risk is contamination rather than direction. Rub both tonsillar pillars and the posterior pharynx without letting the swab touch the tongue, the teeth or the gums.
In both cases, place the swab straight into the transport medium, label it, and send it immediately.

chunks.label: 24-hour urine

chunks.label: Sputum
chunks.body: Cough from the chest - not saliva

chunks.label: Stool for OPC
chunks.body: Three samples on three different days

slides.rationale: Each rule exists to remove a specific source of error: contamination from the first part of the stream, a miscounted collection period, mouth flora instead of lung secretions, and the intermittent shedding of parasites.

slides.heading: Section 2 in brief
slides.design_rationale: A recap specimen by specimen, which is how a nurse will come back to this section - looking up one procedure at a time.

chunks.label: Routine urine: early morning, midstream clean catch, sent within 15–20 minutes.
Urine C/S: sterile container. From a Foley, clamp 20–30 min and aspirate from the port - never the bag.
24-hour urine: discard the first void, record the time, collect every void after it.
Sputum: early morning, rinse the mouth, cough from the chest - not saliva.
Stool OPC three days; OBT needs NSAIDs stopped 7 days and iron 3 days.
CSF is taken by a clinician; you prepare, position, monitor and send immediately.
Swabs: nasopharyngeal parallel to the palate; oropharyngeal avoiding tongue and teeth.

vo: Let us consolidate this section.
A routine urine specimen is early morning, midstream clean catch, and sent within fifteen to twenty minutes.
Urine for culture goes in a sterile container, and from a Foley catheter it is aspirated from the sampling port after clamping for twenty to thirty minutes - never from the drainage bag.
For a twenty-four-hour collection, discard the first void, record that time, and collect every void after it.
Sputum is early morning, after rinsing the mouth, coughed from the chest rather than spat from the mouth.
Stool for ova, parasite and cyst is three samples across three days, and the occult blood test needs NSAIDs stopped for seven days and iron for three.
Cerebrospinal fluid is taken by a clinician - you prepare the articles, position and monitor the patient, and send the specimen immediately.
And a nasopharyngeal swab goes parallel to the palate towards the ear, while an oropharyngeal swab rubs the tonsillar pillars without touching tongue or teeth.
In Section 3 you will learn what happens to the specimen after you have taken it.

objectives.text: State the transport requirement for each specimen type
Identify the critical specimens that need immediate transport
Recognise the complications of blood collection, lumbar puncture and urine collection
Avoid the common errors that cause a specimen to be rejected

slides.heading: Transport, Documentation and Safe Practice
slides.design_rationale: Section cover. A specimen in a transport bag, because this section is about everything that happens between the bedside and the bench.

images.purpose: Labelled specimen in a biohazard transport bag with a requisition form
images.search_terms: specimen transport bag biohazard requisition form

vo: Welcome to Section 3, the final section of the module on Patient Preparation and Specimen Collection.
A correctly taken specimen can still produce a wrong result if it reaches the laboratory late, unlabelled, or in the wrong container.

In this section you will learn the transport requirements, what to document, the complications to watch for, what to teach the patient, how to segregate the waste, and the errors that most often spoil a sample.

slides.heading: Learning objectives
slides.design_rationale: Objectives for the closing section, pitched at the duties that follow collection and apply to every specimen type.

images.purpose: Simple line-art target or goal icon, single colour

candidates.shows: Icon library - pick a single-colour outline target

vo: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
State the transport requirement for each specimen type.
Identify the critical specimens that need immediate transport.
Document a specimen collection completely.
Recognise the complications of blood collection, lumbar puncture and urine collection.
Segregate biomedical waste correctly.
And avoid the common errors that cause a specimen to be rejected.

slides.heading: Transport requirements
slides.design_rationale: Specimen against requirement against reason. The source already had this as a table, correctly - the third column is added because a nurse who knows why CSF is not refrigerated will not refrigerate it at three in the morning.

rows: Delay reduces recovery of the organism
Some organisms do not survive cooling
Bacteria multiply in the container and distort the count
Overnight secretions give a more concentrated sample
Urine, water or menstrual blood will alter the result
On ice if delay is expected
Cooling slows cell metabolism and preserves the values

images.purpose: Specimen in a sealed biohazard transport bag with the requisition form

callouts.text: CSF is the exception that catches people out: immediate, and never refrigerated.

vo: Proper transport preserves the sample. Delays or the wrong storage conditions cause bacterial overgrowth, cell destruction or chemical change, any of which alters the result.
Blood cultures go to the laboratory immediately, because delay reduces the recovery of pathogens.
Cerebrospinal fluid also goes immediately, and must not be refrigerated. CSF is a critical specimen, especially where meningitis is suspected, and some organisms do not survive cooling.
Urine for culture should reach the laboratory within one hour. Beyond that, bacteria multiply in the container and the count is no longer meaningful.
Sputum is best collected early in the morning, when secretions have accumulated overnight, and sent as soon as possible after collection.
Stool for occult blood must be collected without contamination by urine, water or menstrual blood, any of which affects the result.
And arterial blood gas samples are transported on ice if immediate analysis is not possible, because cooling slows cellular metabolism and preserves the oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH values.

slides.heading: Critical specimens
slides.design_rationale: Six specimens where a delay changes a treatment decision rather than just a number. Given their own slide so the learner can recognise one on a tray and move it to the front of the queue.

callouts.text: These six do not wait for the next round. A delayed potassium or troponin postpones a decision that is being made now.

vo: Certain specimens are critical and must reach the laboratory immediately.
Blood cultures, cerebrospinal fluid, arterial blood gases, lactate, troponin and potassium.
A delay in processing any of these produces an inaccurate result and postpones an urgent treatment decision. Prompt transport of a critical specimen is a nursing responsibility, not a porter's.

slides.heading: What to document
slides.design_rationale: Five fields, each one something the laboratory or the next nurse will need. Treated as a named set because documentation is checked off rather than written as prose.

chunks.label: Date and time of collection
chunks.body: Some results depend entirely on the timing

chunks.label: Collector's name
chunks.body: For accountability

chunks.label: Patient preparation
chunks.body: Fasting, medication withheld, collected before antibiotics

chunks.label: Unusual observations
chunks.body: Difficult collection, haemolysis, low volume, patient reaction

callouts.text: Record it in the laboratory register, the nursing notes and the patient's file - all three. One entry in one place is not traceable.

vo: Accurate documentation gives traceability and protects the patient.
Record the date and exact time of collection, because some results depend entirely on when the sample was taken.
Record the type of specimen collected.
Record the name or signature of the person who collected it, for accountability.
Record any special patient preparation - fasting, a medication withheld, collection before antibiotics - because these influence the result.
And record any unusual observation: difficulty collecting the sample, haemolysis, insufficient quantity, contamination, or an adverse reaction such as dizziness or bleeding.
Enter all of it in the laboratory register, the nursing notes and the patient's medical record.

slides.heading: Complications by procedure
slides.design_rationale: Three procedures with distinct complications, grouped so the learner knows what to watch for after each one rather than holding a single undifferentiated list.

rows: Correct technique and firm post-procedure pressure
Lying flat as protocol specifies, and close monitoring
Contamination - bacteria, vaginal secretions, stool, water
Clean catch technique and a sterile container

vo: Specimen collection is generally safe, but complications occur.

During blood collection, the common ones are haematoma from blood leaking into the surrounding tissue, prolonged bleeding, fainting, and rarely infection at the puncture site. Proper technique and firm pressure afterwards prevent most of them.

After a lumbar puncture, the patient may have a post-lumbar-puncture headache, leakage of cerebrospinal fluid from the site, or localised back pain. Close monitoring and correct positioning reduce these.
In urine collection, the common problem is contamination - with bacteria, vaginal secretions, stool or water - which produces an inaccurate result and a repeat test.
Recognising these early is what keeps the patient safe and the investigation accurate.

slides.heading: What to teach the patient
slides.design_rationale: Five teaching points, most of which the patient has to act on when no nurse is present. Their own slide, because a specimen collected at home or unsupervised is only as good as the instruction that preceded it.

chunks.label: The correct collection method
chunks.body: Midstream urine, deep sputum, stool technique

vo: Patient education is a nursing responsibility before any specimen is collected.
Explain the purpose of the test, so the patient understands why it is being done and how it helps.
Give clear fasting instructions, including how long the fast needs to be for tests like blood sugar or a lipid profile.
Tell them about any medication that needs to be withheld temporarily, where the physician has advised it.
Teach the correct collection method - midstream urine, deep sputum, stool technique - so the sample is not contaminated.
And explain why the specimen must reach the laboratory promptly, because delay affects the quality of the sample and the accuracy of the result.

slides.heading: Quality control and infection prevention
slides.design_rationale: Four habits that protect the sample and the handler at the same time. Grouped on one slide because they are performed together, in the same few seconds, at the end of every collection.

callouts.text: Double-checking the label is the last chance to catch an error that the laboratory cannot see and cannot correct.

vo: Quality control and infection prevention run through every collection.
Maintain aseptic technique and avoid touching the sterile areas of equipment or containers, which would contaminate the specimen.
Use clean, intact, leak-proof containers, so nothing spills during transport.
Before sending the specimen, double-check the label for the correct patient details, date and time.
And dispose of used needles, gloves, swabs and other contaminated material according to biomedical waste guidelines.

slides.heading: Biomedical waste segregation
slides.design_rationale: Four colour-coded streams, where the colour is the whole instruction. Icons with the colour named in the label, because this is recalled visually at the bin rather than read.

chunks.label: Yellow bag
chunks.body: Infectious waste - contaminated dressings and swabs

chunks.label: Red bag
chunks.body: Contaminated plastic - tubing, gloves, syringes without needles

chunks.label: White container
chunks.body: Sharps - needles and blades, puncture-proof

chunks.label: Blue container
chunks.body: Broken glassware and medicine vials

images.purpose: Colour-coded biomedical waste bins side by side in a hospital
images.search_terms: colour coded biomedical waste bins hospital segregation

candidates.shows: Waste segregation photos - prefer one showing yellow, red and blue together

callouts.text: A needle in the wrong bag injures whoever handles it next. Sharps go in the puncture-proof white container, at the point of use.

vo: Correct biomedical waste segregation protects healthcare workers and the environment.
Infectious waste, such as contaminated dressings and swabs, goes in the yellow bag.
Contaminated plastic items - tubing, gloves and syringes without needles - go in the red bag.
Sharps, including needles and blades, go in a puncture-proof white container.
And broken glassware and medicine vials go in the blue container.
Correct segregation is a nursing responsibility and a key part of infection control.

slides.heading: Common laboratory abbreviations
slides.design_rationale: Eight abbreviations the learner will read on request forms every day. A two-column table because this is a reference to be scanned rather than a concept to be understood.
vo: These are the abbreviations you will see on request forms every day.
CBC is Complete Blood Count, and KFT is Kidney Function Test.
LFT is Liver Function Test, and C and S is Culture and Sensitivity.
R and E is Routine Examination, and ABG is Arterial Blood Gas.
CSF is Cerebrospinal Fluid, and OBT is Occult Blood Test.

slides.heading: Errors to avoid
slides.design_rationale: Six specific errors, every one of which appears somewhere earlier in the course as a rule. Collected here as a closing checklist, because this is the slide a nurse will screenshot.

chunks.label: Drawing above an IV infusion line
chunks.body: IV fluid dilutes the sample

chunks.label: Underfilling the citrate tube
chunks.body: Coagulation results come out wrong

callouts.text: Never draw from a vein above a running infusion. The result will look like a real one and be diluted.

vo: Finally, the errors that most often spoil a sample.
Do not draw blood from a vein above an intravenous infusion line, because the fluid dilutes the sample.
Fill the citrate tube to the marked level - underfilling produces an incorrect coagulation result.
For sputum, make sure the patient provides deep respiratory secretions rather than saliva.
Always use a sterile container for a culture specimen.
Avoid delays in transport, which alter the composition of the sample.
And give correct fasting instructions, because the wrong ones produce a result that cannot be interpreted.

slides.heading: Check your understanding!
slides.instruction: Select all that apply and click Submit.
slides.design_rationale: Added. Specimens are spoiled by several small omissions at once, so a multi-select asks the learner to recognise a set - which is how the errors appear on a real tray.
slides.question: Which of the following will compromise a specimen you have just collected? Select all that apply.

options.text: Drawing the sample from a vein above a running IV infusion
Refrigerating a CSF sample until the porter arrives
Sending a urine culture to the laboratory two hours after collection
Inverting an EDTA tube gently several times after filling

slides.rationale: A, B and C. IV fluid dilutes the sample, cooling kills organisms that CSF culture depends on, and bacteria multiply in urine left standing beyond an hour. Inverting an EDTA tube is correct practice - it is shaking that causes harm.
vo: Now, let us answer a question to check our understanding.
Which of the following will compromise a specimen you have just collected? Select all that apply, then click Submit.

slides.heading: Key points
slides.design_rationale: The closing recap for the whole course, spanning all three sections rather than this one alone, because this is where the learner finishes.

chunks.label: Pathology investigations support accurate diagnosis, treatment and monitoring.
Most laboratory errors happen before the sample reaches the bench.
Two identifiers, the right container, the right order of draw, the right fill.
Follow the test-specific rules: fasting, timing, asepsis, drug holds.
Blood culture and CSF go immediately; CSF is never refrigerated.
Document time, specimen, collector, preparation and anything unusual.
Teach the patient, segregate the waste, and check the label twice.

vo: Let us summarise the key points of the whole module.
Pathology investigations are essential for accurate diagnosis, treatment planning and monitoring.
Most laboratory errors happen before the sample ever reaches the bench - in the preparation, the collection, the labelling and the transport.
Reliable results depend on correct patient identification with two identifiers, the right container, the correct order of draw and the correct fill level.
Follow the test-specific rules: fasting, timing, aseptic technique and any drug holds.
Blood cultures and cerebrospinal fluid go to the laboratory immediately, and CSF is never refrigerated.
Document the time, the specimen, the collector, the preparation and anything unusual, in the register, the notes and the file.
And teach the patient, segregate the waste correctly, and check the label twice.
Through careful preparation, correct collection and prompt transport, nurses make the laboratory result something a clinician can safely act on.
